main.text: Various interpretations of the word חסידה chasida, or asida.

As רחם racham is named from mercy, so the bird that follows, חסידה hasida, or asida, as some write it with the aspiration dropped, is named from piety. I find a great many interpretations of this word. I. First, the Septuagint translators render it ἐρωδιόν [erōdion], and the Vulgate translator herodium or herodionem, that is, heron, in the Law and in verse nineteen of Psalm one hundred and three (one hundred and four in the Hebrew). Aquila too consistently has ἐρωδιόν [erōdion], as do Symmachus and Theodotion at Zach. V, 9. I also have two manuscript Arabic Psalters, one of which, in the place cited above, has الهيرودي [al-hīrūdī] alheiraudi, τὸν ἐρωδιόν [ton erōdion]. The Ethiopic likewise has ሄሮድዮስ፡ herodios. To the same I refer what stands in the Paris edition of the Psalms, البلشوم [al-balshūm] albalsum. For the bird بلشوم [balshūm] balsum, or بلشون [balshūn] balsun, also called مالك الحزين [mālik al-ḥazīn] malich alhazin, certainly seems to be the heron. This I gather from the descriptions of the Arabs, which run thus. Damir: البلشون هو مالك الحزين [al-balshūn huwa mālik al-ḥazīn] Abalsun is Malich alhazin. Giauhari: مالك [col. 322] الحزين هو طير الما [mālik al-ḥazīn huwa ṭayr al-māʾ] Malich alhazin is a water bird. Ibno Bari in his Marginal Notes: هو طير طويل العنق والرجلين [huwa ṭayr ṭawīl al-ʿunuq wa-l-rijlayn] It is a bird with a long neck and legs. Alkazuinius likewise: طير طويل الرقبة والرجلين يقال له بالفارسية بوتيما [ṭayr ṭawīl al-raqaba wa-l-rijlayn yuqāl lahu bi-l-fārisiyya būtīmā] A bird with a long neck and legs, which in Persian is called BUTHIMA. The same author, and Damir from Algiahid: من اعاجيب الدنيا امر مالك الحزين لانه لا يزال يقعد بقرب الما ومواضع نبعها من الانهار وغيرها فاذا انقصت حزن عليها ويبقي حزينا كييبا وربما ترك الشرب حتي يموت عطشا خوفا من زيادة نقصها بشرب منها [min aʿājīb al-dunyā amr mālik al-ḥazīn li-annahu lā yazālu yaqʿudu bi-qurb al-māʾ wa-mawāḍiʿ nabʿihā min al-anhār wa-ghayrihā fa-idhā anqaṣat ḥazina ʿalayhā wa-yabqā ḥazīnan kayīban wa-rubbamā taraka al-shurb ḥattā yamūta ʿaṭashan khawfan min ziyādat naqṣihā bi-shurbihi minhā] Among the wonders of the world is what they say of malich alhazin: that it always lives by the waters, whether of rivers or springing from elsewhere. When it sees them diminish, this torments it so that it remains sad and sorrowful, and sometimes abstains from drinking so long that it dies of thirst, lest they be diminished too much if it drinks from them. There follows in Damir a not dissimilar fiction about a kind of glow-worm, which the Arabs say shines by night, is winged, green and smooth, flits near rivers and feeds on the dust of the earth, but so sparingly and meagrely that it is never sated and sometimes dies of hunger, fearing the dust of the earth would run out if [III, 79] it ate its fill. These things were invented by the poets as types of the avaricious man, who denies himself what he has taken from others and cheats his own appetite. But truer is what Attaugides reports of the same bird in the book الامتناع والموانسة [al-imtināʿ wa-l-muwānasa] Of Antipathy and Sympathy: مالك الحزين ينشل الحيتان من الما فياكلها وهي طعامها ولا يحسن السباحة فان اخطاه الانتشال وجاع طرح نفسه علي شاطي البحر وفي بعض ضحضاحاته فاذا اجتمع اليه السمك الصغار اسرع في خطف ما استطاع منها [mālik al-ḥazīn yanshilu al-ḥītān min al-māʾ fa-yaʾkuluhā wa-hiya ṭaʿāmuhu wa-lā yuḥsinu al-sibāḥa fa-in akhṭaʾahu al-intishāl wa-jāʿa ṭaraḥa nafsahu ʿalā shāṭiʾ al-baḥr wa-fī baʿḍ ḍaḥḍāḥātihi fa-idhā ijtamaʿa ilayhi al-samak al-ṣighār asraʿa fī khaṭf mā istaṭāʿa minhā] Malich alhazin draws fish out of the waters, on which it feeds, and has them for its food, although it cannot swim. And when it is hungry and this fishing does not succeed, it throws itself from the seashore into the shallows, and from the little fish that approach it snatches with great haste whatever it can. Hence I infer that it is the heron, of which Oppian's paraphrast [Ixeut. book 2, ch. 8] says, in Gesner: They say that getting food from the waters was first discovered by herons, and that the rest learned it from them, since at the beginning all birds had one food. [col. 323] Then, since they gloried in this discovery and boasted that not even Neptune could compete with them in swimming, they lost this art through the god's anger, etc. Hence all other birds plunge into the water to catch fish; but herons, lacking the faculty of swimming, hunt standing on the shore. This mark is most certain, since among water birds there is no other that cannot swim. Here is another mark in Damir, though less explicit: وهو لا يحتاج الي تزواج الاسفاد [wa-huwa lā yaḥtāju ilā tazwāj al-isfād] It does not desire copulation and coition. Namely, because it does not mate without pain. The Philosopher, History, book 9, ch. 1: Τῶν δ’ ἐρωδιῶν ἐστι τρία γένη· ὅ τε πέλλος, καὶ ὁ λευκὸς, καὶ ὁ ἀστερίας καλούμενος. Τούτων ὁ πέλλος χαλεπῶς εὐνάζει τε, καὶ ὀχεύει. κράζει τε γὰρ, καὶ αἷμα, ὥς φασιν, ἀφίησιν ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ὀχεύων. [Tōn d’ erōdiōn esti tria genē; ho te pellos, kai ho leukos, kai ho asterias kaloumenos. Toutōn ho pellos chalepōs eunazei te, kai ocheuei. krazei te gar, kai haima, hōs phasin, aphiēsin ek tōn ophthalmōn ocheuōn.] And again in ch. 18: Τῶν δ’ ἐρωδιῶν ὁ μὲν πέλλος, ὥσπερ εἴρηται, ὀχεύει μὲν χαλεπῶς. [Tōn d’ erōdiōn ho men pellos, hōsper eirētai, ocheuei men chalepōs.] Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 60: Of herons there are three kinds, leucon, asterias, pellos. These suffer distress in coition. The males indeed pour blood from their eyes as they cry out. Accordingly the Etymologicum, and Eustathius on Iliad κ, would have ἐρωδιὸν [erōdion] named παρὰ τὸ ἔαρ, vel ἔωρ, ὃ σημαίνει τὸ αἷμα, καὶ ἰδίειν τὸ ἱδροῦν. ἐν γὰρ ταῖς μίξεσιν (ὥς φασιν) ἡ ἐρωδιὸς αἷμα ἱδροῖ [para to ear, vel eōr, ho sēmainei to haima, kai idiein to hidroun. en gar tais mixesin (hōs phasin) hē erōdios haima hidroi], from ἔαρ [ear] or ἔωρ [eōr], which means blood, and ἰδίειν [idiein], which is to sweat. For the heron, as they say, sweats blood in coition. But I prefer to agree with those who say ἐρωδιὸς [erōdios] is as it were ἐλωδιὸς [elōdios], marsh bird: φιληδεῖ γὰρ τοῖς ἑλώδεσι τόποις [philēdei gar tois helōdesi topois], for it delights in marshy places. Now a third mark follows. The Muslim theologians permit eating the balsun, or malich alhazin; but, as the sons of the physicians assert, لحمه غليظ بارد [III, 80] يولد ادمان اكله البواسير [laḥmuhu ghalīẓ bārid yuwallidu idmān akalihi al-bawāsīr] Its flesh is coarse and cold, and the excrements from eating it produce haemorrhoids. This very thing Arnoldus de Villa-nova teaches about the heron, in Gesner, in these words: Whoever frequently suffers from haemorrhoids, especially throbbing ones, should above all beware, among other things, of cranes and agrones (that is, herons). Certainly, then, بلشوم [balshūm] balsum, or بلشون [balshūn] balsun, is the heron ^{(1)}, which from the fable we have related is called by another name مالك الحزين [mālik al-ḥazīn] malich alhazin, the sad waterer or sad drinker. For ملك [mlk] malch among the Arabs means, among other things, water. I note this here because the lexicographers have omitted the word بلشوم [balshūm] or بلشون [balshūn].

II. Second, חסידה hasida is rendered fulica [coot] by the old translator, whom Augustine and Arnobius follow on the Psalms. But this interpretation arose from the preceding one. For however much the heron and the fulica, or fulix, differ, there have nevertheless been found even among the most learned some who took these birds indiscriminately. Thus in his version of Aratus, Avienus renders τὸν ἐρωδιὸν [ton erōdion] now as fulix, now as ardea. And in the Glosses of Philoxenus you may read: ἐρωδιὸς [erōdios], Erodius, fulica. Pliny too, book 11, chapter 37, stumbling on the same stone, says: "And to the kind of the coots nature has given crests"; which is proper to herons. And in book 10, chapter 44, he makes the Diomedean birds "like coots." Hence Solinus, chapter 2: "Their form is almost that of coots." And Isidore, book 12, chapter 7: "The Diomedean birds" etc. "in form like the coot." But, as a great man observes on Solinus, by the name fulicae Pliny meant erodii. For the Greeks declare that those Diomedean birds are not merely like erodii, but αὐτόχρημα ἐρωδιοὺς [autochrēma erōdious], actually erodii, that is, herons. Aelian, at the very beginning of the History: καλεῖταί τις Διομήδεια νῆσος, καὶ ἐρωδιοὺς ἔχει πολλούς [kaleitai tis Diomēdeia nēsos, kai erōdious echei pollous]. "A certain island, named Diomedea, [col. 324] has many erodii, that is, many herons." Stephanus: Νῆσος ἡ Διομήδεια, ἐν ᾗ οἱ ἐρωδιοὶ χειροήθεις προσπετόμενοι, καὶ εἰς τοὺς κόλπους δύοντες [Nēsos hē Diomēdeia, en hē hoi erōdioi cheiroētheis prospetomenoi, kai eis tous kolpous dyontes]. "The island Diomedea, in which tame erodii fly up and slip into one's lap." Servius on book 11 of the Aeneid: "Hence those birds are to this day called Diomedeae in Latin, which the Greeks call ἐρωδιοὺς [erōdious]. A bird of this kind, he said, Homer reports appeared as an omen to Diomedes and Ulysses as they went scouting:"
Τοῖσι δὲ δεξιὸν ἧκεν ἐρωδιὸν ἔγγυς ὁδοῖο Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη. — — [Toisi de dexion hēken erōdion engys hodoio Pallas Athēnaiē]

And far older than all these is Antigonus, History 48, which needs a physician's hand: Περὶ δὲ τῶν Τώων Λύκον μὲν ἐν τῇ Διομηδείᾳ τῇ νήσῳ φησὶν [III, 81] ἱϛορεῖν τοὺς ἐρωδιοὺς ὑπὸ μὲν τῶν Μήδων, ὅτ᾽ ἂν παραβάλλῃ τις εἰς τοὺς τόπους, οὐ μόνον ψαυομένους ὑπομένειν, ἀλλὰ καὶ προσπετομένους εἰς τοὺς κόλπους ἐνδύνειν, καὶ σαίνειν φιλοφρόνως [Peri de tōn Tōōn Lykon men en tē Diomēdeia tē nēsō phēsin historein tous erōdious hypo men tōn Mēdōn, hot' an paraballē tis eis tous topous, ou monon psauomenous hypomenein, alla kai prospetomenous eis tous kolpous endynein, kai sainein philophronōs]. This should be translated thus: "He says that Lycus, concerning the Trojans (that is, in the Troica), relates that on the Diomedean island the herons, when anyone comes to those places, not only allow themselves to be touched by strangers, but also fly down and slip into their lap, and fawn on them caressingly." Therefore for Τώων [Tōōn] one must write Τρώων [Trōōn], not Κώων [Kōōn], as Xylander would have it. Lycus Butheras of Rhegium, a Peripatetic philosopher, father of Lycophron, had written many histories around the time of Ptolemy son of Lagus, which are mentioned by Agatharchides, Clement of Alexandria, Porphyry, Suidas, both Tzetzes, etc. Among them are the Troica cited here, from which he took occasion to treat of Diomedes and the birds of Diomedes, which he did not say were touched ὑπὸ τῶν Μήδων [hypo tōn Mēdōn], by the Medes, coming to those places. That would have been ridiculous, since the Medes never came there, nor had anything in common with Diomedes. Therefore, for ὑπὸ τῶν Μήδων [hypo tōn Mēdōn], restore ὑπὸ τῶν ἀποδήμων [hypo tōn apodēmōn], or ἐκδήμων [ekdēmōn], by foreigners; to whom are at once opposed the ἐγχώριοι [enchōrioi], the natives. For there follows: Λέγεσθαι δέ τι τοιοῦτον ὑπὸ τῶν ἐγχωρίων, ὡς τῶν τοῦ Διομήδου ἑταίρων εἰς τὴν τῶν ὀρνέων τούτων φύσιν μετασχηματισθέντων [Legesthai de ti toiouton hypo tōn enchōriōn, hōs tōn tou Diomēdou hetairōn eis tēn tōn orneōn toutōn physin metaschēmatisthentōn], "the natives relate that the companions of Diomedes were transformed into the nature of these birds." But this in passing.

III. Third, some of the ancients translated it πελαργὸν [pelargon], stork, whom Olympiodorus on Job tries to refute thus: Ἡ ἀσίδα δὲ ὁ ἐρωδιός ἐστι κατὰ Ἀκύλαν, ἢ ὁ πελαργὸς, ὥς τινες ἔφασαν, οὐ καλῶς νοήσαντες· οὐ γὰρ εἰς γῆν τίκτει ὁ πελαργὸς, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς τὰ ὑψηλὰ τῶν δένδρων. Καὶ οἱ ὀρνιθιακὰ γράψαντες ἕτερον γένος ἔφασαν εἶναι παρὰ τὴν ἀσίδα τὸν πελαργόν [Hē asida de ho erōdios estin kata Akylan, ē ho pelargos, hōs tines ephasan, ou kalōs noēsantes; ou gar eis gēn tiktei ho pelargos, all' eis ta hypsēla tōn dendrōn. Kai hoi ornithiaka grapsantes heteron genos ephasan einai para tēn asida ton pelargon]. "The asida is the ἐρωδιὸς [erōdios], the heron, according to Aquila, or the stork, as some say, who do not judge rightly: for the stork lays its eggs not on the ground but in lofty trees. And those who have written on the nature of birds have taught that the stork is a kind different from the asida." For Suidas, however, ἐρωδιὸς [erōdios] is εἶδος ὀρνέου ὁ πελαργὸς λεγόμενος, ἢ ὅμοιος αὐτῷ [eidos orneou ho pelargos legomenos, ē homoios autō], "Erodios is a kind of bird which is called the stork, or one like it." This could have been tolerated if he had said only like: for in truth the heron and the stork are alike in many respects. Be that as it may, this interpretation pleased the later Hebrews most, for most of whom the hasida is the stork.

IV. Fourth, Symmachus renders חסידה hasida in Job as ὁ κύκνος [ho kyknos], cygnus [swan], a bird that in some respect resembles the heron, the coot and the stork. Accordingly, the Diomedean birds, which some compare with herons and others with coots, Ovid compares with swans, Metamorphoses book 14, fable 10:

If you ask what the form of these doubtful birds is, Though not that of swans, it is very close to white swans. [III, 82] And a Greek author in Phavorinus: Οἱ δὲ φίλοι αὐτοῦ θρηνοῦντες αὐτὸν μετεβλήθησαν εἰς ὄρνεα ὅμοια κύκνοις [Hoi de philoi autou thrēnountes auton metheblēthēsan eis ornea homoia kyknois]· His friends, as they wept for him, were changed into birds like swans. And Isidore, in order to reconcile the various opinions in some way, describes these birds as similar in form to the coot, of the size of swans, white in colour, etc. [col. 325] Yet I doubt whether the bird which others called heron, coot and stork was called a swan by Symmachus in Job because of a likeness of form. And I suspect that the word is corrupt, and that instead of κύκνος [kyknos] we should read ἰκτῖνος [iktinos], that is, kite, as Symmachus rendered it elsewhere, as we shall presently say.

V. Fifth, חסידה hasida is rendered by Jerome as kite in Psalm. CIV, 17. Ierem. VIII, 7. and Zachar. V, 9. And in Letter 135, to Sunnia and Fretela, he declares that in this point he follows Symmachus and the sixth edition. "For herodius (he says), which in Hebrew is called חסידה hasida, "Symmachus translated ἰκτῖνον [iktinon], that is, kite. And so we too have rendered it in Latin: The fir is the house of the kite. Because, namely, it has always been accustomed to make its nests in lofty and steep trees. Hence the sixth edition also translated more plainly: The cypress for the kite to nest in." And again on Ierem. VIII: "For kite, which Symmachus translated" etc. And on Zachar. V: "The Hebrews think the hasida is the kite, a most rapacious bird, always lying in wait for domestic fowl."

VI. Sixth, the older Hebrews explain it as דיה לבנה deja lebana, which I do not interpret with Jerome as kite, but as white vulture. For that דיה daja is the vulture, not the kite, is clear from Es. XXXIV, 15, where the דיות dajoth are said to gather together. This does not suit the kite, but, among birds of prey, the vulture alone, as we showed in its place ^{a)}. Moreover, the Talmudists and the Chaldee paraphrasts divide דיה daja into black and white, a distinction nobody makes for kites, since there is no white kite. But we have dealt at length ^{b)} with the black and the white vulture: of these the former was called above simply דיה daja, the latter רחם racham by Moses. The matter will become clearer from reading the Talmudic passage, which runs thus in the tractate Cholim ch. 3, fol. 63a: אמר רב יהודה החסידה זו דיה לבנה למה נקרא שמה חסידה שעושה חסידות עם חברותיה, Rabbi Judah said: Hasida is the white daja. Why is it called hasida? Because it does hasidoth (kindnesses, that is, acts kindly) with its companions. Namely, as the Gloss there says, מחלקת מזונותיה, sharing its food with them. He sees nothing who does not see that this cannot be said of the kite, which does not admit other kites to share its food, but of vultures, which fly in flocks onto the same carcass. Accordingly [III, 83] דיה is expressly explained as vulture by Solomon [Rashi] in his Notes on Zachar. V, 9. The Chaldee interpreters too follow the same as the Talmudists. And in the Law, Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum have דיותא חווריתא, white vulture. And Onkelos has חווריתא alone, that is, white, supply vulture. So it also occurs in the Chaldee paraphrase of Job and Jeremiah. But Rabbi Joseph the Blind on Psalm. CIV, 17 has ותיא חוריתא. What ותיא means in these words, let him say who can.

VII. Seventh, at Zach. V, 9., for the words They had wings ככנפי החסידה, like the wings of the hasida, the Chaldee has And swift peoples carried them over quickly כמא דמשתרי נשרא, as the eagle flies: as if the hasida were a kind of eagle; that is, following the view of those who take eagles and vultures indiscriminately. Pagninus too, in his larger Lexicon, renders it aquila herodiana [herodian eagle], but for a quite different reason. In the barbarous writers erodius or herodius is not the heron, but the larger and γνήσιος [gnēsios] eagle, or even the so-called hiero-falco. Albertus: The herodius is a very large eagle, entirely black, although in old age the colour on the back and over the wings turns ash-grey, etc. Vincent in the Doctrinale, book 16, chapter 162: The herodius, which is also called girfalchus, is the noblest of all birds, blue in colour, etc. So strong that it catches the eagle, etc. The Gloss on Deuteronomy chapter 14: The herodius is commonly called girfalco, and it seizes the eagle, etc. And on Psalm 103: The herodius is the most rapacious of all the larger birds, [col. 326] and overcomes the eagle. Albertus imagines that it is so called as if the hero of birds. Thus by the word herodius or herodio in the Vulgate version the writers of those times understood either the larger eagle or the gyrfalcon ^{(2)}. Carried away by their torrent, Pagninus fell into the same error.

VIII. I had intended to pursue the remaining interpretations of this word in the same manner. But I fear I may weary the reader if I dwell on each one. For although I have already brought forward many, more still remain. Nothing has yet been said, namely, of the Samaritan [III, 84], for whom the hasida is ࠔࠍࠅࠍࠉࠕࠀ, the swallow ^{(3)}. Nor of those Arabs who in the Law explain it as الصقر [al-ṣaqr] sacrum, the hawk; in the Psalms as الهام [al-hām], the little owl; in the Prophets as القعقع [al-qaʿqaʿ] alkoko, which Gabriel Sionita takes in one place for the crane, in another for the magpie, but wrongly in both, as will be shown below. Nor of the Syriac, which elsewhere renders it ܚܣܝܕܐ, the stork, but in Job ܐܛܐ, the otus. Nor of the Greeks in Zechariah, for whom כנפי החסידה are πτέρυγες ἔποπος [pteryges epopos], the wings of the hoopoe. Nor of Olympiodorus on Jeremiah, where we read Ἰνδικόν ἐστι γένος ὀρνέου ἡ ἀσίδα [Indikon esti genos orneou hē asida], the asida is an Indian kind of bird. Nor of Polychronius on Job, where we read Τινὲς ἔφασαν τὴν Ἀραβίδα εἶναι ὄρνιν, ἥτις ἐν τῇ Μεσοποταμίᾳ εὑρίσκεται [Tines ephasan tēn Arabida einai ornin, hētis en tē Mesopotamia heurisketai], some have held that it is an Arabian bird, which is found in Mesopotamia. Nor of the lexicographers, Cyril and Phavorinus, for whom ἀσίδα [asida] is στρουθοκάμηλος [strouthokamēlos]. Let it suffice to have noted these once and together, so that amid so many waverings of the ancients we may now try to set our foot on firm ground.

This is confirmed even further by Schneider in his Animadversions on the Chapters of Albertus Magnus on Falcons etc. (which are inserted in his Commentaries on the Remains of the Books of Frederick II), p. 92. Moreover, to this class must also be assigned the Syriac Physiologus, recently edited by Tychsen. For it, the ἐρωδιὸς [erōdios] of the Alexandrians (placed by them for the Hebrew חסידה), from whom it took its ܐܪܘܕܝܘܣ (Erodius), is not the heron but, as Tychsen rightly observed, either the falco chrysaetos of Linnaeus or another species not unlike it, since in Chapter 17 it calls its herodius a malicious bird, solitary, by no means gregarious or migratory, which does not devour carrion.

"The swallow, though indeed a messenger of spring and migratory (Ierem. VIII, 7.), is nevertheless quite unsuitable, because its particular dwelling is not tall trees (which is said of the חסידה in Ps. CIV, 17.), but the roofs of houses." So J. D. Michaelis in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 3, p. 861, note, who should by all means be consulted on these ancient interpretations.
